title: Last Item or Minus One
statement:
Add a method last() to every array in JavaScript, so that [1, 2, 3].last() returns 3. It returns the array's final element, or -1 when the array is empty.

The element can be any JSON value, including null. If the last element is null, return null; only an empty array gives -1.

The test harness cannot install methods on Array.prototype, so the tested entry point is lastItem(arr). It must return exactly what arr.last() would. The second solution shows the prototype-style method written with this.

examples.why: The final element is 3; what comes before it does not matter.
No elements, so the fallback -1 is returned.
The array is not empty, so its last element, null, is the answer. A fallback like ?? -1 would wrongly turn it into -1.

hints: Arrays know their own length. Which index holds the final element?
Check emptiness by length, not by looking at the value you got back: a real element can be null, 0 or false.
As a prototype method, the array is available as this. Use a regular function, not an arrow function, so this is bound to the array.

explain.intuition:
Every array inherits from Array.prototype, so a function stored there becomes a method on all arrays. Inside it, this is the array the method was called on, so this[this.length - 1] is the last element.

The trap is the empty case. Shortcuts like this.at(-1) ?? -1 or this[this.length - 1] || -1 decide based on the value, so they turn a real last element of null, 0 or false into -1. Decide based on length instead.
steps: Define last as a regular function (arrow functions do not get their own this).
In real code, install it with Array.prototype.last = last; here, lastItem(arr) calls it as last.call(arr).
pitfalls: Using ?? or || to supply the -1. Both misfire when the last element is null, and || also on 0, "" and false.
Writing the method as an arrow function. Its this is the surrounding scope, not the array.
Returning undefined for an empty array, which is what arr[-1] or arr.at(-1) give.

solutions.title: Check the length, then index
solutions.idea: An empty array gives -1; otherwise the element at index length − 1.

solutions.title: Prototype-style method using this
solutions.idea: Write last() the way it would live on Array.prototype, reading the array from this, and call it with the array bound as this.

followups: Why do style guides warn against adding methods to built-in prototypes? What could break?
Install last() so it does not show up in for...in loops over arrays. Which API controls that?
